overview.text: Gravitational waves are traveling disturbances in spacetime itself, not ordinary light waves or ripples moving through air. Predicted by Einstein’s general theory of relativity, they are produced by changing motions of mass; the strongest detectable signals come from extreme events such as black holes or neutron stars spiraling together. As a wave passes, it changes distances between objects, but the effect is extraordinarily small. LIGO’s first direct detection, in 2015, came from two merging black holes. Gravitational waves carry information from cosmic events and give scientists a new way to study the universe, complementing observations made with light.

key_facts.text: Einstein’s general theory of relativity predicts gravitational waves; direct detection later provided strong evidence for the theory.
When black holes or neutron stars orbit closer together, their system can emit waves that carry away energy.
A passing gravitational wave changes distances between objects; the resulting length changes are extremely small.
LIGO directly detected waves from merging black holes in 2015; the discovery was announced in 2016.
Gravitational-wave observations can be combined with observations of light to study cosmic events in a complementary way.
